propositions.text: This is an application under subsection 22.1(1) of the Citizenship Act for a writ of mandamus to compel processing of citizenship application.
propositions.quote: This is an application under subsection 22.1 (1) of the Citizenship Act, RSC, 1985, c C-29 [the Act] for a writ of mandamus pursuant to section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act, RSC 1985, c F-7. The Applicant seeks to compel the Respondent to process her citizenship application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is an application for a writ of mandamus to compel citizenship application processing.

propositions.text: The determinative issue is the interpretation of section 42 of the IRPA regarding the Applicant's inadmissibility as accompanying family member.
propositions.quote: the determinative issue turns on the interpretation of section 42 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, [IRPA], namely whether the Applicant would be inadmissible as an accompanying family member of her father who is the subject of ongoing admissibility proceedings.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the key issue as interpreting IRPA section 42 on Applicant's inadmissibility as accompanying family member.

propositions.text: Applicant came to Canada as permanent resident with parents on October 5, 2006; parents accepted under business visa, Applicant accompanying member.
propositions.quote: The Applicant came to Canada with her parents on October 5, 2006 as a permanent resident; her parents were accepted to Canada under the business visa category, and she was an accompanying member.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant arrived in Canada as a permanent resident accompanying her parents under business visa.

propositions.text: Applicant began citizenship process in March 2015; application processing completed except for final oath step.
propositions.quote: In March 2015, she began the process of obtaining her Canadian citizenship. The processing of her application has proceeded through all steps and awaits only the final step of taking her oath.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Applicant started citizenship process in 2015 and awaits only the oath.

propositions.text: Respondent suspended Applicant's citizenship application processing on September 14, 2015 under subsection 13.1(a) to investigate admissibility hearing or removal order.
propositions.quote: the Respondent suspended the processing of the Applicant’s citizenship application pursuant to subsection 13.1 (a) of the Act, in order to receive information on whether she should be the subject of an admissibility hearing or a removal order under the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Respondent suspended Applicant's citizenship processing to investigate admissibility or removal.

propositions.text: Section 13.1 of the Act allows Minister to suspend application processing to receive information on admissibility or removal under IRPA.
propositions.quote: Section 13.1 of the Act reads as follows: 13.1 The Minister may suspend the processing of an application for as long as is necessary to receive ... whether the applicant should be the subject of an admissibility hearing or a removal order under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

paragraphs.summary: The court quotes section 13.1 allowing suspension of application processing to receive admissibility information.

propositions.text: Applicant's citizenship application suspended pending outcome of father's admissibility proceedings for alleged IRPA violations before permanent residency.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s citizenship application was suspended pending the outcome of her father’s admissibility proceedings with respect to matters that occurred before he became a permanent resident said to be in violation of sections 36(1) (serious criminality), 37(1) (organized criminality), and 40(1) (misrepresentation)of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Applicant's application suspended pending father's admissibility proceedings for alleged IRPA violations.

propositions.text: If Applicant's father found inadmissible, Applicant would be inadmissible as accompanying family member under subsection 42(1)(b) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: the Respondent originally submitted that should the Applicant’s father be found to be inadmissible, then she would be inadmissible on grounds of being an accompanying family member pursuant to subsection 42(1)(b) of the IRPA

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Applicant would be inadmissible as accompanying family member if father found inadmissible under IRPA 42(1)(b).

propositions.text: Subsection 42(1)(b) does not apply to Applicant as permanent resident; it applies only to foreign nationals excluding permanent residents.
propositions.quote: the Applicant submitted that subsection 42(1)(b) does not apply to her as a permanent resident, because the provision only applies to foreign nationals. The term foreign national is defined in the IRPA to exclude permanent residents.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues subsection 42(1)(b) excludes permanent residents like her, applying only to foreign nationals.

propositions.text: Court finds subsection 42(1) likely does not apply to Applicant as she is a permanent resident, excluded as foreign national by IRPA definition or French wording.
propositions.quote: it appeared highly likely that subsection 42(1) would not apply to the Applicant inasmuch as she is a permanent resident. Either in the English wording of the provision by the definition under the IRPA, she is not a foreign national; or by the French wording of the subsection she would be specifically excluded, i.e. “sauf pour le résident permanent”.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds subsection 42(1) likely inapplicable to Applicant as permanent resident excluded from foreign national definition.

propositions.text: At hearing end, Respondent sought to certify a question and permission to file further submissions on subsection 42(1), which was granted.
propositions.quote: At the termination of the hearing, when the issue of certifying a question for appeal was raised, the Respondent indicated that it wished to certify a question, and also sought permission to file further submissions on the applicability of subsection 42(1), which was granted.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Respondent sought and was granted permission to file further submissions on subsection 42(1).

propositions.text: Respondent argued no certified question needed; admissibility proceedings against Applicant on misrepresentation would render her inadmissible per Wang decision.
propositions.quote: the Minister argued that a certified question was not necessary because the admissibility proceedings against the Applicant, if successful on the ground of misrepresentation pursuant to paragraph 40(1)(a), would render her inadmissible in accordance with the decision of Justice O’Keefe in Wang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FC 1059 [Wang].

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues admissibility proceedings on misrepresentation would render Applicant inadmissible per Wang, no certified question needed.

propositions.text: Paragraphs 40(1)(a) and (b) define inadmissibility for misrepresentation for permanent residents or foreign nationals.
propositions.quote: Paragraphs 40(1)(a) and (b) read as follows: 40 (1) A permanent resident or a foreign national is inadmissible for misrepresentation ...

paragraphs.summary: Court quotes paragraphs 40(1)(a) and (b) defining inadmissibility for misrepresentation.

propositions.text: Facts here analogous to Wang where husband's misrepresentation attributed to spouse as indirect misrepresentation, a constructive misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: The facts in this matter are analogous to those in Wang, except that there the admissibility proceedings were undertaken against both the spouse and husband on account of the husband’s misrepresentation. The Court concluded that the husband’s misrepresentation was attributable to the applicant as “indirectly misrepresenting” material facts...

paragraphs.summary: Court finds facts analogous to Wang where indirect misrepresentation was attributed to spouse as constructive misrepresentation.

propositions.text: Respondent argues if father found inadmissible for misrepresentation, a section 44 Report will be made against Applicant leading to admissibility hearing and likely exclusion order.
propositions.quote: The Respondent now argues that upon the father being found inadmissible on the ground of misrepresentation, a section 44 Report will be made against the Applicant. The matter would be referred to the Immigration Division for an admissibility hearing where she would likely be found inadmissible for indirect misrepresentation in accordance with the Wang decision.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues a section 44 Report against Applicant would lead to admissibility hearing and likely exclusion order if father found inadmissible.

propositions.text: Court accepts scenario except rejects section 42's bearing on Applicant's removal; direct inadmissibility under 40(1)(a) suffices for removal.
propositions.quote: The Court accepts the logic of the foregoing scenario, except for the submission that section 42 has any bearing on the Applicant’s removal. In the eventuality of her being found to have made an indirect misrepresentation, the Applicant would be determined to be inadmissible pursuant to subsection 40(1)(a). This would render her directly subject to removal without any need to consider her removal as a foreign national pursuant to section 42

paragraphs.summary: Court accepts scenario but finds section 42 irrelevant; direct inadmissibility under 40(1)(a) suffices for removal.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Court should not entertain new submission on section 40 as it is separate ground; evidence shows sole ground is section 42 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: She urges the Court not to entertain the new submission regarding section 40 because it is an entirely separate ground. The Applicant argues that the evidence in the Certified Tribunal Record indicates that the sole alleged ground for her inadmissibility is the triggering of section 13.1 of the Act via section 42 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Court should not consider new section 40 submission as sole inadmissibility ground is section 42.

propositions.text: Court allowed Applicant to file further submissions on section 40 despite reservations, but criticizes delay and procedural conduct.
propositions.quote: the Court allowed the Applicant to file further submissions, inasmuch as it is obvious that she was required to consider the new argument of the application of paragraph 40(1)(a) to the facts of the case. However, the Court’s displeasure stems from the fact that a party should not advance an argument, while holding back an alternative submission in the hope that it may succeed on the first ground.

paragraphs.summary: Court allowed further submissions on section 40 but criticizes Applicant's procedural conduct causing delay.

propositions.text: Applicant submits section 44 Report applies only if made directly against her, not as accompanying dependent; she is not subject of admissibility proceeding.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that a section 44 Report on inadmissibility could only apply if the Report was made directly against her, and not as an accompanying dependent of her father who is not a foreign national.

propositions.text: Court rejects Applicant's argument, interpreting section 13.1 to allow suspension if applicant should be subject of admissibility hearing; indirect misrepresentation applies.
propositions.quote: The Court does not agree with this submission, which turns on the interpretation of section 13.1 of the Act. It allows the Minister to suspend the citizenship proceedings when the circumstances arise of “whether the applicant should be the subject of an admissibility hearing or a removal order”... her situation would be one where she should be the subject of an admissibility hearing if her father is found to be inadmissible on grounds of a misrepresentation.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues section 44 Report applies only if directly against her; Court rejects, interpreting section 13.1 to allow suspension for admissibility hearing.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Court should adopt Stanizai decision finding no statutory authority to pause citizenship application pending cessation proceedings.
propositions.quote: the Applicant also argues that it should adopt the decision in Stanizai v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 74 [Stanizai]. The Court in Stanizai found that there was no statutory authority for the Citizenship and Immigration Canada [CIC] to put the applicant’s citizenship application “on pause” until the cessation proceedings had been concluded against him.

propositions.text: Court rejects Applicant's argument, distinguishing Stanizai as predating section 13.1's statutory authority for suspension.
propositions.quote: this decision was rendered on facts arising prior to section 13.1 (2014, c. 22, s. 11.) having application, and must be distinguished on the basis that there now exists statutory authority for the suspension of the citizenship proceedings as described above.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant urges adoption of Stanizai decision; Court rejects, distinguishing it due to new statutory authority in section 13.1.

propositions.text: Is the Court required to entertain the Respondent’s new submissions and should it do so as a discretionary matter?
propositions.quote: First, is the Court required to entertain the Respondent’s new submissions, and if not, should it entertain them in any event as an exercise of its discretion.

propositions.text: Does Wang apply to this matter and does it remain good law?
propositions.quote: Second, does Wang apply to the circumstances in this matter, and if so, does it remain good law?

propositions.text: All four questions must be answered affirmatively despite harsh consequences for the Applicant unless humanitarian relief applies.
propositions.quote: The Court concludes that all four questions must be answered in the affirmative, even though the personal consequences for the Applicant seem harsh, unless relieved on humanitarian grounds.

propositions.text: The Court is required to entertain the Respondent’s new submissions.
propositions.quote: (1) The Court is required to entertain the Respondent’s new submissions

paragraphs.summary: The Court identifies two issues about entertaining Respondent's new submissions and Wang's applicability, concluding affirmatively on all four questions including entertaining submissions.

propositions.text: Parties must introduce evidence forming factual basis; Court decides on facts and law fairly, subject to appeals.
propositions.quote: The general rule in the Court’s adversarial regime is that the parties are required to introduce the evidence before the Court, which forms the basis for its factual conclusions.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states parties must introduce evidence, but it decides on facts and law fairly, subject to appeal rights.

propositions.text: Minister's submissions on constructive misrepresentation lack evidentiary support and are speculative.
propositions.quote: the Minister was making “submissions that were not supported by the evidence in this matter”.

propositions.text: Only evidence of investigation under section 42 IRPA exists; Respondent cannot raise speculative new grounds.
propositions.quote: the sole evidence of any direct investigation of inadmissibility being conducted by the Minister against the Applicant is under section 42 of the IRPA. The Respondent is not free to raise a speculative new ground of investigation which the evidence does not indicate

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Minister's submissions lack evidence and that only section 42 IRPA investigation evidence exists, so new grounds are speculative.

propositions.text: Officer's affidavit expresses intention to proceed based on law, not actual historical facts.
propositions.quote: The Court does not agree with the characterization of the relevant affidavit evidence of the Officer as relating to actual or historical facts, as opposed to the expression of an intention of proceeding on those facts based on the Officer’s understanding of the applicable law.

propositions.text: Officer's affidavit recounts suspension of Applicant's citizenship application pending father's admissibility proceedings under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s affidavit recounted that the Applicant’s application for citizenship was suspended under section 13.1 of the Act pending the outcome of her father’s admissibility proceedings, pursuant to the various sections cited of the IRPA

propositions.text: If father found inadmissible, Applicant falls under section 42 IRPA as accompanying family member.
propositions.quote: In the event her father is found inadmissible the Applicant falls under the purview of section 42 of the IRPA − accompanying family member of an inadmissible person

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer's affidavit expresses intention to proceed legally, recounts suspension pending father's admissibility, and notes Applicant falls under section 42 if father inadmissible.

propositions.text: Affidavit facts concern father's admissibility; references to section 42 proceedings are intentions, not binding evidence.
propositions.quote: The only relevant facts in the affidavit concerned the father’s admissibility proceedings. Reference to proceedings that would follow pursuant to section 42 of the IRPA are statements of intention and are not binding on the Court as evidence

propositions.text: References raise procedural fairness and ability to respond to new argument issues.
propositions.quote: They raise only an issue of procedural fairness and being able to respond to a new argument.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds affidavit facts concern father's admissibility; references to section 42 are intentions raising procedural fairness issues.

propositions.text: Respondent raised paragraph 40(1)(a) issue; Applicant initially did not respond to avoid confronting legal effect.
propositions.quote: The Respondent has placed the issue of the applicability of paragraph 40(1)(a) before the Court and the Applicant first chose not to respond, hoping to avoid having to confront the legal effect of the provision.

propositions.text: Applicant did not claim procedural prejudice from Respondent's late argument change.
propositions.quote: The Applicant has not claimed prejudice, as this term is used in the procedural sense when a party is taken by surprise without the ability to properly respond in the circumstances.

propositions.text: Court has no procedural fairness concerns about Applicant's opportunity to respond to new legal submissions.
propositions.quote: the Court has no concerns about any procedural fairness in the Applicant not having had an opportunity to fully respond to the Respondent’s new legal submissions applying to the facts.

propositions.text: Constructive misrepresentation is relevant to inadmissibility and must be considered in decision.
propositions.quote: Given the factual foundation, the constructive misrepresentation issue is a relevant facet of inadmissibility law and must be considered by the Court in rendering its decision.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Respondent raised paragraph 40(1)(a); Applicant did not claim prejudice; Court sees no procedural fairness issue; constructive misrepresentation is relevant.

propositions.text: Court would refuse further evidence only if Applicant suffers uncompensable prejudice.
propositions.quote: In exercising any discretion to allow the issue to be heard, if that were the case in these circumstances, such as the Respondent requesting to file further relevant evidence, the Court would only refuse to permit this if the Applicant was placed in a position that it would suffer a prejudice that could not be compensated for by costs.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states it would refuse further evidence only if Applicant suffers prejudice not compensable by costs.

propositions.text: Wang's interpretation of 'indirectly misrepresenting' is generally accepted and applied in other cases.
propositions.quote: the interpretation of “indirectly misrepresenting” in Wang has been applied in other cases, and is therefore generally accepted by the Court.

propositions.text: Applicant made further submissions challenging Wang's applicability.
propositions.quote: the Applicant has made further submissions regarding the issues that it raises

propositions.text: Court will review Wang's reasoning to ensure applicability to this matter.
propositions.quote: the Court will review the underlying reasoning in Wang to ensure its applicability to the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes Wang's interpretation is accepted; Applicant challenges it; Court will review Wang's reasoning for applicability.

propositions.text: Golden rule of purposive interpretation requires reading Act's words in context, ordinary sense, harmoniously with scheme and intent.
propositions.quote: Justice O’Keefe applied the golden rule of purposive interpretation, being that “[t]oday there is only one principle or approach, namely, the words of an Act are to be read in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament”

paragraphs.summary: Justice O’Keefe applied the golden rule of purposive interpretation requiring reading Act's words in context and intent.

propositions.text: Wang noted subsection 40(1)(a) replaced unambiguous former subsection 22(1)(e) with ambiguous 'indirectly misrepresenting'.
propositions.quote: Justice O’Keefe noted the somewhat unusual state of the remedial legislation by the enactment of subsection 40(1)(a) in the IRPA, whereby the ambiguous phrase “indirectly misrepresenting” replaced the unambiguous construction in former subsection 22(1)(e) of the Immigration Act

propositions.text: Former Immigration Act referred to misrepresentation by applicant or any other person.
propositions.quote: Under the Immigration Act, the reference was made to misrepresentation of any material fact “whether exercised by [the Applicant] or by any other person”.

paragraphs.summary: Wang noted subsection 40(1)(a) replaced unambiguous former subsection 22(1)(e) referring to misrepresentation by applicant or others.

propositions.text: Clause by clause analysis of Bill C-11 emphasized section 40 modifies provisions to enhance enforcement against abuse.
propositions.quote: section 40 was “similar to provisions of the current act concerning misrepresentation[…] but modifies those provisions to enhance enforcement tools designed to eliminate abuse”

propositions.text: Parliament intended to strengthen inadmissibility in IRPA as per clause by clause analysis.
propositions.quote: When Parliament introduced the new IRPA, one of the objects of the Act was to strengthen inadmissibility as seen in the clause by clause analysis prepared for IRPA

paragraphs.summary: Clause by clause analysis shows section 40 enhances enforcement to eliminate abuse; Parliament intended to strengthen inadmissibility.

propositions.text: Not adopting constructive misrepresentation leads to absurdity where innocent accompanying persons are not removable.
propositions.quote: not adopting an interpretation of constructive misrepresentation applying to other persons “would lead to a potential absurdity that an applicant could directly misrepresent an application and bring a person such as the applicant in with him or her, and that person would then not be removable from Canada if the person had no knowledge of the misrepresentation”

propositions.text: Objective of reducing abuse supports constructive misrepresentation interpretation.
propositions.quote: the objective of reducing the potential for abuse would be a purpose of the provision, as may be extrapolated from the extrinsic interpretative evidence cited above.

paragraphs.summary: Wang found not adopting constructive misrepresentation leads to absurdity; Court agrees abuse reduction supports this interpretation.

propositions.text: Word 'indirectly' covers relying on inclusion in application without knowledge of misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: the word “indirectly” can be interpreted to cover the situation “where the applicant relied on being included in her husband’s application, even though she did not know his being married with a son”

propositions.text: This meaning is analogous to principal-agent relationship where principal is responsible for agent's conduct.
propositions.quote: This scenario is somewhat analogous to the principal-agent relationship in contract law, where the principal is indirectly held responsible for the direct conduct of the agent.

paragraphs.summary: Wang interprets 'indirectly' to cover reliance without knowledge; Court finds analogy to principal-agent responsibility.

propositions.text: Removing fault, responsibility arises from benefiting from misrepresentation, leading to absurdity if allowed.
propositions.quote: When fault is removed as an element of the misrepresentation, responsibility leads back to the Applicant via a constructive interpretation as the person not only relying on, but also benefiting from the misrepresentation.

propositions.text: Abuse arises when parent confers permanent residency benefit on child who would not be admitted otherwise.
propositions.quote: The abuse arises from the potential of a parent wishing to confer the benefit of permanent residency on the child, even if the parent is removed.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds responsibility arises from benefiting from misrepresentation; abuse arises when parent confers residency benefit on child.

propositions.text: Paragraph 40(1)(b) supports interpretation that sponsored persons are inadmissible if sponsor is inadmissible for misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: It provides that a permanent resident or a foreign national is inadmissible for misrepresentation “for being or having been sponsored by a person who is determined to be inadmissible for misrepresentation”.

propositions.text: Underlying purpose is to avoid abuse by benefiting from misrepresentation, supporting inadmissibility of sponsored persons.
propositions.quote: The same objective of avoiding abuse by obtaining a benefit from a misrepresentation would appear to be the underlying purpose that supports the person being sponsored to be found inadmissible.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds paragraph 40(1)(b) supports avoiding abuse by benefiting from misrepresentation, making sponsored persons inadmissible.

propositions.text: Section 42 deals with accompanying family members exempted from removal due to principal's inadmissibility.
propositions.quote: the provision specifically deals with the issue of accompanying family members who are permanent residents being exempted from removal on account of the inadmissibility of the principal family member.

propositions.text: Given ambiguity of 'indirectly misrepresenting', analysis should consider section 42 contextually.
propositions.quote: given the acknowledged ambiguity of “indirectly misrepresenting”, the analysis may not be complete without considering this contextual provision.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes section 42 exempts accompanying family members from removal and that ambiguity requires contextual consideration of section 42.

propositions.text: Section 42 applies only where principal's misconduct occurs after obtaining permanent residency.
propositions.quote: it is the Court’s view that the provision is intended to apply only where the misconduct of the principal family member... occurs after obtaining permanent residency.

propositions.text: Without this, absurdity arises in differing treatment of accompanying family members based on misconduct type and timing.
propositions.quote: Without this distinction there is an apparent absurdity in the differing treatment of accompanying family members based upon whether the principal family member’s conduct was a misrepresentation, as opposed to a rise because of serious criminality or organized criminality.

propositions.text: If principal misrepresents, accompanying family member removed; if serious crime, accompanying permanent resident stays due to section 42.
propositions.quote: If the conduct involves a misrepresentation of the principal family member, the accompanying family member would be removed... Conversely, the accompanying permanent resident family member of a person who commits a serious criminal act... would stay because section 42 would apply to exempt him or her from removal

paragraphs.summary: Court finds section 42 applies only if principal's misconduct occurs after residency; otherwise, differing treatment causes absurdity.

propositions.text: Omitting serious criminality in residency application is direct misrepresentation by omission.
propositions.quote: omitting to advise CIC of previous serious criminality or organized criminality in an application for permanent residency would constitute a direct misrepresentation by omission.

propositions.text: Accompanying family members of such persons are inadmissible under paragraph 40(1)(a) for indirect misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: the accompanying family members of these persons would also be found to be inadmissible under paragraph 40(1)(a) for indirectly misrepresenting the omitted facts.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds omission of serious criminality is direct misrepresentation; accompanying family members are inadmissible under paragraph 40(1)(a).

propositions.text: Section 42 applies only if misconduct occurs after family members gain permanent residency in Canada.
propositions.quote: subsection 42 only applies if the misconduct of misrepresentation, serious criminality or organized criminality occurs after the family members gain permanent residency while in Canada.

propositions.text: Paragraph 40(1)(a) applies only to misrepresentations made before permanent residency is obtained.
propositions.quote: paragraph 40(1)(a) would not apply because only misrepresentations made prior to achieving permanent residency would concern “material facts relating to a relevant matter that induces or could induce an error in the administration of this Act”.

propositions.text: Serious criminality after residency causes inadmissibility of principal but not accompanying family members.
propositions.quote: Conduct of serious criminality or organized criminality that occurs after the person gains permanent residency would give rise to a conclusion of inadmissibility of the individual responsible for the misconduct, but not the accompanying family members.

propositions.text: Accompanying family members did not gain residency by misconduct before entering Canada.
propositions.quote: They would not have gained permanent residency by any misconduct of any person before entering Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds section 42 applies if misconduct occurs after residency; paragraph 40(1)(a) applies before residency; serious crime after residency affects principal only.

propositions.text: Officer’s affidavit states inadmissibility sections relate to father's misconduct before he became permanent resident.
propositions.quote: It mentions that the inadmissibility sections related to the father’s misconduct apply “to matters that occurred before he became a permanent resident”.

propositions.text: Parliament concluded no basis to remove permanent resident accompanying family members who did not gain status by principal's misconduct.
propositions.quote: It would appear that Parliament concluded that there is no basis for removing permanent resident accompanying family members because they did not gain that status by means of the misconduct of the principal family member, thus no potential for abuse occurs.

propositions.text: Foreign nationals remain inadmissible reflecting higher status of permanent residents.
propositions.quote: The distinction made whereby foreign nationals would nevertheless be inadmissible appears to reflect the higher status of permanent resident, as opposed to the foreign national who has no status at all.

paragraphs.summary: Officer’s affidavit notes father's misconduct before residency; Parliament concluded no removal basis for permanent resident family members; foreign nationals remain inadmissible.

propositions.text: The ratio in Wang applies to this matter's circumstances.
propositions.quote: the Court concludes that the ratio in Wang applies to the circumstances of this matter.

propositions.text: If Applicant's father misrepresented a material fact under subsection 40(1)(a) IRPA, Applicant will be inadmissible for indirectly making the same misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: there is a high likelihood that if the Applicant’s father should be found to have misrepresented a material fact with respect to matters described in subsection 40(1)(a) of the IRPA, she will constructively be determined to be inadmissible for “indirectly” making the same material misrepresentation.

propositions.text: This result satisfies section 13.1 of the Act allowing suspension of Applicant's citizenship processing pending admissibility hearing determination.
propositions.quote: This result meets the requirements of section 13.1 of the Act that allows for the suspension of the processing of the Applicant’s citizenship application pending the determination of whether she should be the subject of an admissibility hearing under the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Wang applies, that Applicant may be inadmissible if her father misrepresented facts, and that suspension of citizenship processing is allowed under section 13.1.

propositions.text: The Court dismisses the application for writ of mandamus requiring Respondent to complete Applicant's citizenship processing within three months.
propositions.quote: The Court dismisses the application for a writ of mandamus requiring the Respondent to complete the processing of the Applicant’s application for Canadian citizenship in accordance with the Act and to undertake any other formalities necessary to grant citizenship to the Applicant within three (3) months of this Judgment.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for mandamus to require citizenship processing within three months.

propositions.text: No certification of questions for appeal was requested or will be certified.
propositions.quote: No certification of questions for appeal was requested; none will be certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court states no appeal questions were requested or certified.

propositions.text: No costs were requested or ordered; application dismissed without costs and no appeal questions certified.
propositions.quote: No costs were requested and none are ordered. JUDGMENT FOR T-363-17 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that the application is dismissed without costs and no question is certified for appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court orders no costs and dismisses the application without costs or appeal questions.
